<reason>B won by controlling the decisive frame: justification for coercive transfer must be intrinsic to the destination, because a comparison keyed to the sender's own threatened cruelties has no floor and empties "safe" of meaning. A's best counter (finite adjudicative capacity makes "hear the claim yourself" unavailable) was raised once and never developed, while A's own list of "real alternatives" (pushbacks, offshore camps) fed B's bootstrapping critique. B also gave the trio a principled stopping point (three distinct harms coercion inflicts: legal, economic, personal), blunting the arbitrariness attack, answered both pressure questions directly and honestly, and closed intact with a genuine flip of A's "legislate overnight" point. A landed real analytic hits — the subsistence-vs-work decoupling and the non-splitting-vs-reunification distinction genuinely dented the necessity of two of the three rights — and asked the sharper questions. But A never nailed B's internal tension (paper amendments vs. its own Turkey critique), left its "graded standard" underspecified, and was clipped in four of five turns including the closing's final line, a real execution cost against B's fully landed close.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1 caught A's own baseline containing "some means to challenge removal errors," converting A's absolutism charge into a scope dispute over which enforceable rights count — reframing the whole debate on B's terms. Runner-up: B5.1's closing flip of A4.4 ("the low bar is the point" — a state that won't meet a nearly costless threshold confesses the transfer was about disposal), which turned A's best late attack into evidence for the motion.</best_rebuttal>
